sections.heading: What actually fits in 50 KB?
paragraphs: 50 KB is enough for one clear page, and not much more. A single A4 certificate scanned in colour usually gets under 50 KB once its images are brought down to around 70–100 DPI, which still reads fine on a screen.

A 10-page colour scan is a different story. Every page is a photo of paper, and ten photos rarely fit in 50 KB while staying readable. If a form asks for a multi-page document under 50 KB, check whether it really wants all pages. Often only the first page is needed — use Split PDF to keep it, then compress that page alone.

sections.heading: How the compressor reaches 50 KB
paragraphs: The tool runs Ghostscript, a long-trusted PDF engine, compiled to WebAssembly so it works inside your browser. It starts by redrawing the scanned images at 150 DPI and checks the size. If the file is still above 50 KB, it tries again at a lower resolution, stepping down to 40 DPI at the lowest.

Typed text and vector lines stay sharp at every step, because only the pictures inside the PDF are resampled. If even 40 DPI cannot get under 50 KB, you get a clear message instead of a broken file, and the smallest version is still offered. If your PDF is already under 50 KB, you get the original back untouched.

sections.heading: Tips when the file won't go below 50 KB
bullets: Turn on Black & white. A grey-scale page has far less data than a colour one, and most certificates don't need colour.
Crop the white border before you scan or photograph. Empty margins still cost bytes.
Rescan at a lower setting. A page scanned at 600 DPI carries data that compression later has to throw away anyway; 150–200 DPI is plenty.
Shoot in daylight on a dark table. An evenly lit white page compresses far better than one with shadows and paper texture.
Remove pages the form doesn't need with Split PDF before compressing.

sections.heading: Is 50 KB measured as 50,000 or 51,200 bytes?
paragraphs: Portals differ. Some count 1 KB as 1,000 bytes, others as 1,024. Aim for the stricter number: a file under 50,000 bytes passes both checks. The result card shows the exact size so you can confirm before uploading.

faqs.q: Can I compress a PDF to 50 KB without losing quality?
faqs.a: Partly. Typed text stays crisp because it is kept as text, not pixels, but scanned images lose some detail, since that is where the size comes from. For a single certificate page the result is normally still easy to read on screen. Check the file once before you upload it.

faqs.a: Each scanned page is an image, and eight images rarely fit in 50 KB while staying legible. Ask whether the form needs every page. If it doesn't, split out the required page first. If it does, switch on Black & white, which usually saves the most.

faqs.q: Is my certificate uploaded to your server?
faqs.a: No. The compressor runs inside your browser using WebAssembly. Your PDF is read and written on your own phone or computer and never sent anywhere. You can even switch off mobile data after the page loads and the tool still works.

faqs.q: Will a 50 KB PDF be rejected for being blurry?
faqs.a: It can be, if the original was a dark or tilted phone photo. Compression cannot add detail that was never captured. Rescan in good light, flat and straight, and the 50 KB version will be much clearer. Black & white mode also makes faint text more readable.

faqs.q: Does this work on Android and iPhone?
faqs.a: Yes. It runs in Chrome, Safari or any modern mobile browser with no app to install. Very large PDFs may take longer on older phones, because all the work happens on your device rather than on a server.
